name: Selective omission
statement: Selective omission is a name for material dropped from a shared account, whether by a state retelling its history or an editor choosing what to run.
meaning: The name covers two claims, and this page has to say which. In collective memory it means a group, a government or a press keeping unwelcome episodes out of the story it tells about itself. In media literacy it means a journalist leaving a fact or a whole story out. Neither sense has a research literature under this name. Memory research works on the first idea under other headings, and it has its own word for the gaps a speaker leaves in a retelling. Cuc, Koppel and Hirst called those gaps silences, and Coman, Manier and Hirst use that word for them. Media research works on the second idea as gatekeeping bias, coverage bias and omission bias. The phrase selective omission does appear in the scholarly literature, and in a different job. Crossref returns it as a clinical term for leaving out a test or a treatment in chosen patients, and as a cartographic term for dropping features from a map as its scale shrinks. The entry that follows is about the label, because the label is what exists.

origin.who: Yug, an editor of the English Wikipedia
origin.note: The article Selective omission was created on 21 August 2011, and no earlier use of the phrase as the name of a bias turned up in the searches described under limits. Maintenance templates added in September 2011 flag it for thin sourcing and doubtful notability, and they are still on the page. Its definition hangs on one citation, printed as Penebaker 1997 p79-81. The source list at the foot of the same article gives page 303 of that book, spells the name Pennebaker, and names Routledge as the publisher, where the Internet Archive's record of the 1997 edition gives Lawrence Erlbaum Associates of Mahwah, New Jersey.

evidence: No experiment measures selective omission. The article that names it cites two works. The first is Pennebaker, Páez and Rimé's 1997 collection on the collective memory of political events, which was not obtained here. The second is Brown and colleagues' 2009 paper in Psychological Science, and its subject is the dating of personal memories rather than omission. Its abstract reports that Bosnians often mentioned their civil war and that Turks in Izmit often mentioned the 1999 earthquake when dating mundane events. Serbs, Montenegrins, Turks in Ankara, Canadians, Danes and Israelis rarely mentioned public events at all, and historical references were absent from the protocols collected in New York City after September 2001. The authors conclude that personal significance and not historical importance decides whether a public event organises autobiographical memory. Two measured literatures sit beside the label. On the memory side, what a speaker leaves out of a retelling is studied as socially shared retrieval-induced forgetting. Coman, Manier and Hirst put a questionnaire about 11 September 2001 to 20 New Yorkers, grouped the answers into category and exemplar sets, and then had an interviewer rehearse some answers and not others. On a later recognition test, reaction times were quicker for unpractised items from unpractised categories than for unpractised items from practised ones, t(19) = 2.30, p < .04, d = 0.56. Their second experiment replaced the interview with a free conversation of about seven minutes between 22 unrelated participants in pairs. Listeners showed the same pattern for their own memories, which the speaker had never heard, t(16) = 2.61, p < .02, d = 0.52, and speakers showed it too, t(18) = 2.63, p < .02, d = 0.56. Abel and Bäuml ran four experiments on the same design with word material, 80 subjects in pairs in the first two and 96 in the last two. On cued recall in the first, listeners recalled 60.14% of unpractised unrelated items against 49.14% of unpractised related ones, t(39) = 2.87, p = .007, d = 0.45, and speakers 57.38% against 46.01%, t(39) = 2.58, p = .014, d = 0.41. Their abstract reports the listener effect holding when output order at test was controlled, and shrinking relative to the speaker effect on tests of item recognition. On the media side, D'Alessio and Allen meta-analysed 59 quantitative studies of partisan bias in American presidential campaign coverage since 1948, yielding 132 measurements. They separate gatekeeping bias, the choice of which stories to run, from coverage bias and statement bias. Five studies allowed gatekeeping to be measured as stories per outlet per counted campaign event, and the average across them was d' = -.052, standard error .065, homogeneous and not different from zero. They report no study of gatekeeping bias in network television news. Across all three kinds of bias, all media and all elections, the grand mean was d' = -.018 weighted and -.021 unweighted, standard error .024.

replication.headline: Nothing has been repeated because nothing was run under this name; the nearest measured result is that details a speaker leaves out of a retelling become harder for the listener to recall, d = 0.45 among 80 people tested in pairs.
replication.detail: Selective omission has no paradigm, no measure and no experiment, so there is nothing for a replication to repeat. The two literatures quoted above are cited for what they measured, and neither used the term. Socially shared retrieval-induced forgetting is the better attested of the two. Abel and Bäuml describe their first experiment as replicating prior reports of the effect on category-cued recall, and their four experiments give listener effects of d = 0.45 upwards on 80 and 96 subjects. The Coman experiments are much smaller, at 20 and 22 participants, and they report reaction times rather than recall because they doubted a single conversation would move flashbulb memories at all.

limits: The label is an entry in a bias list, not a construct, and the two senses it spans do not share a method. Searches for it as a psychological or media-studies term covered Crossref, Europe PMC, English Wikipedia's List of cognitive biases and web search. Crossref's bibliographic search returns oncology, transplant surgery, colorectal surgery and road-network cartography for the phrase, and a Europe PMC search for it alongside memory, recall, narrative, collective memory, media and journalism returned clinical papers about omitting treatments. The term does not appear in the List of cognitive biases. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar refused requests during this task and were not searched, and Google Books returned 404 for the preview page the Wikipedia article links to, so the Pennebaker collection was not opened and nothing is quoted from it. The evidence borrowed from elsewhere carries its own limits. Cuc, Koppel and Hirst's 2007 paper, which named the silences and first showed the listener effect, is paywalled and was not obtained; it reaches this page through Coman and colleagues' description of it and through Abel and Bäuml's. The forgetting experiments run on pairs of strangers over minutes in a laboratory, and measure a shift of a few percentage points in recall of practised material. Nothing in them measures a state, a newspaper or a generation. D'Alessio and Allen say plainly that gatekeeping bias is mostly unmeasurable, because the population of stories that might have been covered is unidentifiable, and that their five studies work only where campaign events could be counted. Their zero is about partisan direction summed across outlets, and they name the Washington Times, the Indianapolis Star and the Great Falls Tribune as individual papers with large biases that cancel in the aggregate. Spinde and colleagues' taxonomy of media bias, which sets out gatekeeping, coverage, statement and omission bias, is an arXiv preprint and was read as its HTML version.
misreadings: The first error is to read this as omission bias, which is a separate finding with its own entry. Spranca, Minsk and Baron's effect is a moral judgement, that harm through inaction is rated less bad than the same harm through action. Selective omission is about what goes missing from an account, and the shared word is doing all the work. The second error is to treat the Wikipedia article's evidence as evidence for its claim. Brown and colleagues asked people to date everyday events and found that only populations hit hard and long by a public event used it as a landmark, which says nothing about a group suppressing an unwelcome memory. The third is to read D'Alessio and Allen's zero as a finding that news outlets do not leave things out. Their result is that American newspaper campaign coverage showed no net partisan tilt, and their own text calls the absolute amount of gatekeeping unknowable. The fourth is to treat socially shared retrieval-induced forgetting as the mechanism of national forgetting. It is a laboratory effect in which one person's selective recall makes a listener's unmentioned related memories harder to reach, and the leap from that to a textbook omitting an atrocity is a leap nobody has measured. The fifth is confusion with two entries here that describe different things. Levelling and sharpening is the loss of detail as a story passes down a chain of tellers, and selective amnesia is a clinical term for partial recall of a single episode.
